source.title_on_document: Generative Al as a Collaborative Screenwriting Tool Measuring Creative Output Quality VS. Human-Authored Scripts

supplement.where: The text cites 'Appendix A' for the prompt templates (PDF p. 3, Section II.B); no appendix appears in the PDF and no URL is given.
supplement.holds: Standardized prompt templates used to generate the AI scripts. The paper does not say it holds any statistics.

paper_design_summary: The authors built a corpus of short film scripts (one scene per premise) in four genres under three authorship conditions on matched premises: written by professional screenwriters, generated by a GPT-series model in one pass with minimal editing, or generated and then refined over up to five rounds of critique from a human editor. Industry professionals (screenwriters, script editors, development executives) scored the anonymized scripts blind on a script-coverage rubric (narrative coherence, character depth, dialogue authenticity, thematic complexity, emotional resonance), and conditions were compared by one-way ANOVA. No people were randomly assigned to AI assistance, and the paper gives no count of scripts, writers, editors, or evaluators.

studies.label: Script corpus in three authorship conditions, blind expert rubric scoring

assignment.what_was_assigned: Authorship condition of each script (human-only, AI-minimal, iterative human-AI), with premise and genre matched across conditions; no people were assigned to conditions.
assignment.quote: Proposed mixed-methods workflow (see Fig. 1) model uses matched conditions of genre and premise in 3 parallel branches: human-only, AI-minimal intervention and iterative human-AI collaboration.

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Scripts written by professional screenwriters with no AI involvement.

arms.name: AI-minimal
arms.description: Scripts generated by a GPT-series model in a single pass from a system prompt and the premise, with minimal editing.

arms.name: Iterative Human-AI
arms.description: Scripts generated by a GPT-series model and refined over up to five feedback-refinement iterations, in which a human editor supplies qualitative critiques and the model revises the draft.

participants.exclusions: Not stated. The paper gives no number of scripts, screenwriters, human editors, or evaluators; it says only that the corpus has 'the same numbers of screenplays per condition' and calls the evaluator sample 'moderate'.
participants.who: Human-only scripts by professional screenwriters; iterative scripts refined with a human editor (number and background not stated); scripts rated by screenwriters, script editors, and development executives working in the industry.
participants.quote: Judging was done in blind testing by screenwriters, script editors and development executives all working in the industry.
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (proc. p. 1099), Sections II.B and II.D; PDF p. 6 (proc. p. 1102), Section IV ('Moderate sample size of evaluators')

ai_tool.name_model: Unnamed 'GPT-series' large language models run on a cloud inference engine
ai_tool.how_used: The model writes the whole script. In the AI-minimal arm it generates in one pass with minimal edits; in the iterative arm a human editor critiques each draft and the model rewrites it, up to five rounds (Eq. 2 and Eq. 3, PDF pp. 2-3).

task.description: Short film scripts, one scene per premise, on matched premises in four genres (drama, thriller, comedy, sci-fi).
task.duration: Table 5 (labeled 'hypothetical LLM backend') lists human effort of 120 min per human-only script, 5 min per AI-minimal script, and 25 min per iterative script (PDF p. 5).

outcomes.name: Overall rubric score (Overall Average)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Weighted sum of rubric domain scores (Eq. 4: R = w1 Mnc + w2 Mcd + w3 Mda + w4 Mtc; weights not reported) given blind by industry screenwriters, script editors, and development executives on an adapted script-coverage rubric, apparently on a 0-10 scale. Table 2 reports the overall score by genre (Drama 8.6 / 6.1 / 8.4; Thriller 8.3 / 6.8 / 8.1; Comedy 8.5 / 5.9 / 8.2; Sci-Fi 8.4 / 6.4 / 8.3 for human-only / AI-minimal / iterative). Tables 3 and 4 report the overall score by number of refinement iterations within the AI arms.

contrasts.reported: Overall Average: Human-only 8.42, AI-minimal 6.26, Iterative Human-AI 8.20; Significance '*' (one-way ANOVA across conditions, p < 0.05). No SDs, Ns, or test statistics.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (proc. p. 1100), Table 1; test described PDF p. 3, Section II.D, Eq. 6

contrasts.reported: Overall Average: Iterative Human-AI 8.20 vs Human-only 8.42; text: 'The collaboration with iterative (8.20) and human-only (8.42) contributions is very similar'. The '*' in Table 1 refers to the test across all three conditions; no pairwise test for this contrast is printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (proc. p. 1100), Table 1 and Section III.A-B

contrasts.reported: Overall Average: Iterative Human-AI 8.20 vs AI-minimal 6.26 (Table 1, '*' across conditions). Table 3: Overall Score 6.8 (1 iteration), 7.9 (3), 8.2 (5). Table 4: Overall Quality Score 6.3 (Minimal, 0 edits), 7.6 (Medium, 2 edits), 8.3 (Deep, 4+ edits). No tests for Tables 3 and 4.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (proc. p. 1100), Table 1; PDF p. 5 (proc. p. 1101), Tables 3 and 4

company_involvement.description: Authors list industry affiliations (Zero Density Inc, USA; CapitalOne Bank, USA); the paper names no company role in the study and no funding.

eligibility.reason: Scripts, not people, are placed in authorship conditions: professional screenwriters write the human-only scripts and a GPT-series model writes the AI scripts, with or without critiques from a human editor. No person is randomly assigned to AI assistance. The paper reports no count of scripts, writers, editors, or evaluators. Outcomes are blind expert rubric scores of the scripts.

one_line_finding: Blind industry raters scored single-pass GPT scripts lower than professional human scripts overall (6.26 vs 8.42) and iteratively human-edited GPT scripts near the human level (8.20), with similar narrative coherence across conditions (8.9, 8.7, 8.8; n.s.) (PDF p. 4, Table 1).
open_questions: The paper gives no number of scripts per condition, screenwriters, human editors, or evaluators, and no SDs or test statistics; only significance markers from a one-way ANOVA across the three conditions.

The iterative human-AI arm involves a human editor working with the model, but the editor is not a randomly assigned participant and the number of editors is not stated; I coded the study as ai_vs_human and the iterative contrasts as comparison_type 'other' and question 'none'.
notes: Internal inconsistencies: Eq. 4 defines four rubric domains (Mtc combines thematic complexity and emotional resonance) while Table 1 reports five; Figure 5 caption ('Quality Scores vs. Number of Collaboration Iterations') does not match its content (overall quality and percent improvement by condition); Table 1 headers cite references [13] and [14] next to 'Human-only' and 'AI-minimal', and Table 2 cites [15] and [16], which are unrelated papers; Table 4 deep refinement (8.3) and minimal (6.3) differ slightly from Table 1 (8.20, 6.26). Section II.A calls the setup a 'controlled simulation environment', and Section IV says scripts were 'produced in a virtual setting' and that effort metrics are hypothetical. Table 5 and Figure 6 report generation time and human effort (not creativity outcomes; not listed). A thematic analysis of evaluator comments is qualitative and not listed. Appendix A (prompt templates) is cited but absent.
